basis.text: Berdan's report of 29 July 1863 (27 days after) puts Birney's order at about 11 a. m.; Birney's sworn account of 1864 puts his request for leave at about 11. The order to the detachment is the start; no source gives the minute the men moved off.

default.label: About 11:00 on Jul 2: Berdan is ordered to send the detachment out
default.note: The detachment is drawn leaving not before 11:00; skirmishing a mile west of Round Top is reported at 11:45 to 11:55 by the signal station. Noon and 11:15 stay selectable.

It does not name the sharpshooters, and the corps' picket line was also out in that direction, so it is read as a bound on the start, not as the detachment itself.

positions.label: Before 9:00: Wilcox puts the fight with the Third Maine and the Sharpshooters before his brigade's 9 a.m. line

inference.step: Wilcox writes that the brigade "now (9 a. m.)" took its line after the 15-20 minute fight with the Third Maine and the First New York Sharpshooters; the fight is therefore read as before 9 a. m. by his count. His sentence dates the line, not the fight.

reason_not_chosen.text: No other writer puts the fight before about 11: Berdan, Birney, Hunt and the signal station of the day all place it between about 11 and noon. Wilcox's 9 a.m. stands alone.

weighing.summary: Berdan, who received the order, says about 11 a.m. Birney, who gave it, dates his request for leave at about 11 in sworn testimony of 1864 and Sickles's permission at 12 m. in his report of 1863 (both can be true, so the order may have followed a grant before noon, but Berdan puts his order at about 11); Hunt's sworn testimony has Sickles deciding to send the sharpshooters only after about 11 and a ride out to the line; Hunt's about 12 m. is a second-hand hour from a man who reached the ground about 2. A signal station reported the enemy's skirmishers advancing at 11.45 and the rebels in force, our skirmishers giving way, at 11.55; two sharpshooters' diary entries headed noon have the fight on or over. Noon as the start sits badly with all of that. The start is taken to mean the order to the detachment: about 11:00, weighted, documented by Berdan's own report. No source states the minute the men stepped off; Wilcox's 9 a.m. is one stray hour.
weighing.who: Berdan commanded the detachment and received the order; Birney gave it (on Sickles's leave); Hunt was at headquarters and reached the ground about 2 p. m., so he relays. Jerome was the signal officer on Round Top and saw the skirmishing. Wilcox commanded the Alabama brigade that met the detachment. Marble and Garrett were sharpshooters; Buchanan, who printed their diary entries in 1889, was a lieutenant of the same regiment. The Maine commission's volume (1898) and the New York commission's narrative (1900) are later writers who name no witness for their hours.
weighing.when: Berdan wrote 27 days after (rank 5), Birney's report 36 days after and his testimony eight months after, Hunt 87 days after, Wilcox 15 days after: all reports of the best class. The signal messages are of the day (rank 6). The diary entries are of the day but are seen only as printed 26 to 39 years later. Stevens (1892), the Maine volume (1898) and the New York narrative (1900) are later. The better class of writing than Berdan's report is only the signal messages, and they do not name the detachment; they do not contradict about 11 and they are why noon cannot be the start.
weighing.where: Berdan was with the detachment and got the order; Birney was on the line and sent it; Hunt was elsewhere at the time. Jerome watched from the left end of the line, a mile from the woods. Wilcox was in his own line to the west.
weighing.how_knew: Berdan and Birney knew by the order itself (given and received). Hunt names no source. Jerome saw the skirmishing. The diarists were in it. The two commission writers name no source.
weighing.clock: All the Union writers use the army's clock (signal messages carry their own stamped times). Wilcox's is the Confederate clock; the reported 20-minute difference between the armies is not applied and could not turn 9 into 11 in any case. "At 12 m." is a round figure that may stand for the quarter hour around it; "about 11" is read as 11:00 plus or minus 15 minutes, which is why 11:15 is not excluded but is not stated by anyone either.
weighing.independence: The hour of the order, 11:00, rests on Berdan alone, so the default is flagged single-source; Birney's testimony dates only his request for leave about 11 and Hunt's only that Sickles decided after about 11. Noon rests on Birney's report and Hunt (who did not see it); Stevens names no source and is a group of his own. Birney's two accounts are not shown to contradict each other. The signal messages are one line. Wilcox's 9 a.m. is one man. The Maine and New York volumes of 1898 and 1900 are later writers whose own sources are not named.

source_panel_text: About 11:00 on Jul 2: Colonel Berdan's own report has the order about 11 a.m., and Birney's sworn account of 1864 puts his request for leave at about 11. Birney's report and Hunt's say noon, but a signal station reported skirmishing at 11:45 and 11:55. 11:15 has no source. Seven other values are listed.
